McClure's Magazine. Founded in 1893 by S.S. McClure, it became the flagship publication of the muckraking movement. McClure pioneered the ten-cent magazine price point, which achieved mass circulation of over 400,000 copies. The magazine became famous for muckraking, a term coined partly through McClure's aggressive investigative journalism exposing corruption. One of its most groundbreaking achievements was publishing Ida B. Tarbell's investigation of Standard Oil's monopolistic practices from 1902 to 1904, which contributed to the company's breakup. McClure's also published Lincoln Steffens' investigations of municipal corruption in his work called The Shame of the Cities. The magazine was known for serializing fiction alongside hard-hitting journalism. It attracted major writers including Willa Cather. The editorial mission was explicit: expose wrongdoing and mobilize public opinion toward reform. McClure's declined after the 1910s as muckraking fell out of favor and other magazines captured the investigative mantle. The publication pioneered the long-form exposé format and influenced trust-busting and regulatory reform during the Progressive Era.
